summary: Describes how identity information is represented in the POLICY_DATA object so RSVP can do policy-based admission control. It is a standards-track document, and it was replaced by RFC 3182.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a name tag attached to a reservation so the network knows who is asking.

questions: how to represent identity in rsvp
how to attach credentials to rsvp messages
subtitle: Attaching identity credentials to RSVP reservation requests.

tldr.problem: RSVP allows networks to reserve resources for specific applications, but routers need to know who is asking in order to enforce access control policies. There was no standard way to securely attach identity information to reservation requests.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2752 defines how to encode identity and authentication credentials inside RSVP policy data objects. It supports simple text identifiers, Kerberos tickets, and X.509 digital certificates, allowing routers to authenticate the request and make policy decisions based on user identity or application type.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now enforce identity-based policies for quality-of-service reservations. This RFC was later superseded by RFC 3182 with refinements, but the core approach for binding identity to RSVP messages remains foundational.

facts.label: Supports
facts.value: Digital signatures and encrypted policy locators

today: RFC 3182 superseded RFC 2752 with clarifications and additional identity representation mechanisms. RFC 2752 remains important as the original specification for encoding identity in RSVP policy control.

sections.title: Why Identity in RSVP
sections.content:
RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol) lets applications request quality-of-service guarantees from the network, such as bandwidth or low latency. Networks want to grant these reservations fairly: perhaps premium users get priority, or only work applications get access during business hours. To enforce these policies, routers need to know who is making each request.

RFC 2752 solves this by defining how to securely attach identity information and credentials to RSVP reservation messages. Routers can then authenticate the request, look up the user in a policy database, and decide whether to grant the reservation.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP asks the network for special treatment (faster speed). The network says: OK, but first prove who you are. RFC 2752 explains how to attach that proof to the request.

sections.title: The Policy Data Object Format
sections.content:
RSVP messages carry a POLICY_DATA object that contains policy information. RFC 2752 defines a new type of policy element inside POLICY_DATA called AUTH_DATA (authentication data). The AUTH_DATA element is a list of authentication attributes, each with a type, subtype, length, and value.

Every AUTH_DATA element also has a P-Type (policy element type) field that indicates whether it carries user identity (AUTH_USER) or application identity (AUTH_APP). This allows routers to apply different policies for different types of identities.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP messages have a special section for policy information. RFC 2752 defines what authentication information goes in that section: a type (user or app), length, and the identity data.

sections.title: Authentication Methods
sections.content:
The RFC defines three main authentication methods. Simple text authentication sends the user's login ID in plain ASCII or Unicode, suitable for basic directory lookups. Kerberos authentication sends a Kerberos ticket from a trusted key distribution center, proving the user's identity to a network that also runs Kerberos. Public key authentication sends a digital certificate (X.509 V3, PGP, or other formats), allowing the request to be digitally signed.

Each credential type is encoded as a CREDENTIAL attribute with an A-Type field (CREDENTIAL) and a SubType field specifying which authentication method. For public key methods, a separate DIGITAL_SIGNATURE attribute contains the signature that proves the request was not tampered with in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: You can prove your identity three ways: say your login name, show a Kerberos ticket (if your network uses Kerberos), or sign the request with a digital certificate.

sections.title: Policy Locators and Error Codes
sections.content:
Each AUTH_DATA element can include a POLICY_LOCATOR attribute that points to the policy rules that apply. The locator is usually an X.500 distinguished name (DN) that identifies the policy database entry for that user or application. It can be sent as plain text, as Unicode, or encrypted for confidentiality.

If a router rejects a reservation due to policy violations, it can include a POLICY_ERROR_OBJECT attribute in the error message, with error codes such as unsupported credential type, insufficient privileges, or expired credential. This tells the application why the reservation was denied.
sections.plainLanguage: The identity information can point to a policy file that says what this user is allowed to do. If the request is denied, the network can send back an error code explaining why (for example, credentials expired).

sections.title: Putting It All Together
sections.content:
When a host wants to make a reservation, its RSVP process inserts an AUTH_DATA policy element into the PATH or RESV message. The host either includes a simple ASCII login ID, obtains a Kerberos ticket from a key distribution center, or signs the request with a digital certificate.

When a router receives the message, it extracts the AUTH_DATA element, verifies the credentials (checking the Kerberos ticket against the KDC, or verifying the digital signature), looks up the user or application in its policy database using the POLICY_LOCATOR, and makes an admission decision. If admission is denied, it generates a PATH_ERROR or RESV_ERROR message with the POLICY_ERROR_OBJECT explaining the reason.
sections.plainLanguage: When your app wants to reserve bandwidth, it attaches an AUTH_DATA object with your identity. The router checks if you are really who you say you are, looks up your policy, and decides yes or no. If no, it sends back an error message.
